whatItIs.text: The seed of a stone-fruit tree — botanically not a true nut but a drupe like its cousin the peach, with a hard shell around the kernel.

historyNote.text: Almonds were among the earliest domesticated fruit trees, because they breed true from seed; domesticated-almond remains show up in Early Bronze Age sites of the Middle East. California now supplies about 80% of the world's almonds.

howToChoose.text: Choose whole or sliced almonds that smell sweet and nutty, never sharp or paint-like (that is rancidity); vacuum-sealed or bulk-bin turnover matters more than brand.

storage.text: Refrigerate if you will keep them long — almonds store for around a year chilled but go rancid faster at room temperature.

useItUp.text: Almonds go rancid through oxidation, and toasting will not hide it: a bitter, painty, or crayon-like smell means the bag goes out, not into a recipe. Use them while they still snap and smell sweet — toasted for snacks and salads, blitzed into frangipane, almond milk, or a crust for fish — and store the rest airtight, cool, and dark to slow staling.

substitutions.note: softer, sweeter; similar fat for baking
